what: Installed Building Products installs insulation in new houses. Crews from its branch network arrive after the frame is up and before the drywall, and fit fibreglass, spray foam or cellulose insulation. It also installs garage doors, rain gutters, shower doors, shelving and fireplaces, which are sold to the same builders on the same site visit.
customers: Homebuilders, from the national production builders to local custom builders, plus a growing share of commercial construction work.
money: Installed insulation in new residential construction, the core and most profitable service.
Garage doors, gutters, shower enclosures, closet shelving, fireplaces and commercial work.
moat: This is a logistics and labour business, not a product one. Builders care about a crew arriving on the scheduled day with the right material, because a delay stops every trade behind it. IBP’s branch density and relationships with the national builders are what make that possible, and installation work is bought on reliability rather than price. Material rebates from the big insulation manufacturers also favour whoever installs the most.
risks: Demand is single-family housing starts, and nothing management does changes that. High mortgage rates slow the builders, and IBP’s revenue follows with a lag of a quarter or two.
Revenue growth has flattened: $2.8B in 2023, $2.9B in 2024, $3.0B in 2025.
Fifteen analysts average a $237.33 target, only about 7% above the current price, so very little upside is priced in even by the optimists.
The shares trade at about 25 times earnings for a business whose end market is cyclical and currently soft.
Labour is the main cost and the main constraint: installer wages have risen faster than prices in several markets, and crews are hard to find.
opportunities: Revenue has grown every year shown, from $2.0B in 2021 to $3.0B in 2025, including through a sharp rise in mortgage rates.
Energy codes keep tightening, which raises the amount of insulation required per house regardless of how many houses are built.
The complementary products strategy means each additional service sold to an existing builder relationship adds revenue with almost no new customer acquisition cost.
Free cash flow of $245.2M against a $6.2B market value funds both acquisitions of local installers and buybacks.
A fall in mortgage rates would restart single-family construction, and IBP is geared directly to it.
watch: Single-family housing starts, and price per job. Volumes come from the builders; whether IBP holds its pricing while installer wages rise is the part that is within its control.
view: The best thing about Installed Building Products is that it is not a product company pretending to be a service company. It sells the arrival of a crew with the right material on the right day, which sounds mundane until you consider that a builder loses money every day the drywall cannot go up. That is why installation is bought on reliability and why branch density, scheduling and crew retention are the real competitive assets. It is also why the margins are better than people expect from something that looks like contracting.

The energy code point is the underappreciated part of the story. Building codes in the United States keep raising the insulation required per square foot, which means the amount of work per house rises over time independent of how many houses get built. That gives IBP a slow structural tailwind underneath a violently cyclical end market, and it is the reason revenue grew from $2.0 billion to $3.0 billion straight through the sharpest rise in mortgage rates in forty years. A pure volume play on housing starts would not have done that.

Which brings me to the price, and here I am less enthusiastic. At 25 times earnings with revenue growth flattening to roughly 3% and fifteen analysts seeing only 7% upside, the market is already paying for the quality rather than for the cycle. That is an awkward place to buy a housing-linked business. The upside case requires mortgage rates to fall and single-family starts to recover, which is entirely plausible but is also what everyone owning this stock is already waiting for. Meanwhile installer wages have been rising faster than job prices in several markets, which is the quiet way margins in a labour business get eaten.

So: a genuinely good company, correctly identified as such by the market, in a sector where the entry point matters enormously. I would rather own this at 15 times trough earnings in the depths of a housing downturn than at 25 times flat earnings while waiting for a rate cut that may take another year. The thing worth tracking, beyond the obvious housing starts data, is price per job against labour cost — that ratio tells you whether the reliability advantage is translating into pricing power or merely into market share.
bull: Mortgage rates fall, single-family starts recover, and tightening energy codes mean each house needs more insulation than the last — operating leverage on a franchise that already grew through the downturn.
bear: Rates stay high, starts stay flat, installer wages keep rising faster than job prices, and 25 times earnings meets a business growing 3% with margins under quiet pressure.
